meta.description: A science-literacy workshop: judge the quality of fictional studies with the criteria scientists use, predict the target rating and get expert feedback.

welcome.intro: 'Chocolate makes you smarter.' Headlines promise miracles and warn of disasters, but how good is the research behind them?
welcome.about: In this workshop you read short descriptions of studies and judge their quality with six criteria that scientists use: Title, Access, Source, Theory, Methods & Data and Conclusion.
welcome.fictional: The studies are fictional. They were written for this workshop and are modelled on the strengths and flaws of real research, but none of them describes a real study.
welcome.tasksIntro: For each study you give two answers on a scale from 1 (very low quality) to 7 (very high quality):
welcome.taskPredict: Predict the target rating. This is the answer you score points for. The target is explained below.
welcome.taskRate: Give your own rating. Judge the study yourself with the six criteria. Your own rating does not change your score, but it becomes part of the target for the participants who rate the study after you.
welcome.scoringTarget: Every study has a rating from an expert. The target combines that expert rating, counted as if {weight} people had given it, with the ratings that other participants have given the same study so far. Your own rating is left out of your target.
welcome.scoringEarly: Because the expert counts so heavily, the target stays close to the expert's rating. Even with {count} ratings from other participants, the expert's rating makes up {share} of the target.
welcome.scoringPoints: A prediction that matches the target exactly scores 100 points. You lose {penalty} points for every point you are away from the target, so a prediction 1 point away scores {one} and one 2 points away scores {two}.
welcome.scoringFeedback: After each study you see your score, the target and how it was worked out, and the expert's feedback on each of the six criteria.
welcome.leaderboardText: Your results appear on a public leaderboard under a random nickname, such as 'Curious Otter 42'. Participants are ranked by their average score per study once they have rated at least {minRank} studies. There are {total} studies, and you can finish whenever you like after rating {minFinish}.
welcome.leaderboardRoom: You joined the workshop room {room}. Your results page shows the ranking for this workshop as well as the ranking for everyone.
welcome.dataCollected: We store your ratings and predictions, your scores, how long you spent on each study, when you gave each answer, your random nickname and random codes that identify this browser's session. We do not ask for your name, email address or any other personal details.
welcome.dataNoTracking: There are no analytics or tracking cookies. Your progress is kept in this browser's storage so that you can reload the page without losing it.
welcome.dataUse: The data are pseudonymous: the random codes link your answers to each other but not to you. By taking part you agree that your answers can be used, shared and published for research on how people judge the quality of research. Your nickname and scores appear on the public leaderboard and dashboard.

guide.heading: Before you begin
guide.intro: Take your time with the glossary and the rubric. They explain the terms in the studies and the six criteria you will judge them by. You can open both again from any study with the 'Glossary and rubric' button.
guide.glossaryIntro: Terms you will meet in the studies.
guide.rubricIntro: Use these six criteria to judge each study, then weigh them up to reach your overall rating from 1 to 7. You may give some criteria more weight than others.

results.reviewIntro: The answers for each study, in the order they were given, with the expert's feedback.
results.takeawayAccess: Open access and open data let anyone check the work. They are good signs, but not proof of quality on their own.
results.takeawayHype: Spotting hype: an overstated title is a warning sign, not a verdict. Check whether the methods and conclusion support it.
results.takeawayMethods: Methods matter: sample size, a fair comparison group and open data carry much of the weight when you judge a study.
results.takeawaySource: Source credibility: predatory journals publish almost anything for a fee, and reports from companies may have a conflict of interest.
results.takeawayConclusion: Careful conclusions: good studies say what they cannot show. Be wary of claims that go beyond the data, such as treating a correlation as proof of cause.
results.takeawayCompare: Comparing judgements: after each study you saw the expert's rating and the other participants' ratings. Where yours differed, the criterion notes show what the expert weighed differently.
results.exploreIntro: When you read about research in the news:
results.exploreData: check whether the data are available
results.exploreClaims: ask whether the conclusion fits the evidence
results.exploreSource: consider who published the study and who paid for it
